extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, policy analysts, and financial regulators (agency staff and policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and procedural guidance on how federal financial regulators (e.g., SEC, CFTC, FSOC) should conduct and improve regulatory cost-benefit/economic analysis, including institutional arrangements and best practices. Focuses on elements of analysis, institutional capacity, inter-agency coordination, and metrics of analytical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four basic elements of a good regulatory economic analysis (SEC guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action; (2) the definition of a baseline against which to measure the likely economic consequences of the proposed regulation; (3) the identification of alternative regulatory approaches; and (4) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—both quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives identified by the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list is presented as the SEC’s articulation of the “basic elements of a good regulatory economic analysis,” drawn from Executive Branch guidance. The SEC delves into each element with further explanation (e.g., discussing market failures to justify the need, emphasizing both quantitative and qualitative benefits/costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular A-4 baseline-and-elements requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: [A] good regulatory analysis should include the following three basic elements: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives identified by the analysis. The Circular adds that it is necessary to '[i]dentify a baseline' to properly assess costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular A-4 is a foundational Executive Branch standard repeatedly cited; it requires identifying a baseline and treating the number/choice of alternatives as a matter of judgment, balancing thoroughness and practical analytical limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and justify the relevant market failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory explanations should identify market failures the rule seeks to address (examples cited include market power, externalities, principal-agent problems, and asymmetric information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use invocation of typical market failures to justify the need for intervention; SEC and Circular A-4 list similar failures as customary rationales for rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and number of regulatory alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The number and choice of alternatives selected for detailed analysis is a matter of judgment and should strike a balance between thoroughness and the practical limits on analytical capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular A-4 (quoted by SEC) frames alternative selection as discretionary but subject to a reasonableness constraint — agencies must balance completeness with resource limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define a clear baseline for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must identify a baseline against which to measure the likely economic consequences (costs and benefits) of the proposed regulation and alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The baseline is necessary for proper assessment; failure to identify a clear baseline was a criticism leveled at some CFTC analyses (per Commissioner O’Malia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate benefits and costs both quantitatively and qualitatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analysis should present evaluations of benefits and costs that include quantitative estimates where feasible and qualitative considerations where quantification is difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both SEC guidance and Circular A-4 emphasize quantitative and qualitative treatment. The Committee on Capital Markets Regulation and others have praised more quantitative, detailed analyses as signs of improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate coherent, centralized economic analysis in rule preambles
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic Analysis should appear as a distinct, coherent section of a rule preamble instead of being scattered across multiple sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SEC added an 'Economic Analysis' section to the preamble to provide a focused, coherent presentation of the agency’s economic reasoning and cost-benefit work; this institutional choice is presented as a best practice for clarity and defensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in internal economics capacity and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should build internal expertise (e.g., hiring Ph.D. economists) and better integrate economists into rulemaking processes to improve the sophistication and credibility of analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the SEC’s hiring surge (e.g., 16 Ph.D. economists in 2012; 72 listed later), and recommended by models such as EPA’s experience. Internal capacity is linked to greater use of quantitative methods and improved analysis quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative analysis, length, detail, and quality as indicators of better CBA
rubrics_metrics.description: Improved practice is indicated by increased use of quantitative cost-benefit analysis and by greater length, detail, and quality of the economic discussion in rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee on Capital Markets Regulation’s study measured post-MOU improvements by increases in the proportion of rules with quantitative analysis (e.g., 34.2% to 69.6%), and by longer/more detailed economic sections. The report cautions about methodological limits in such studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with statutory requirement to 'consider' and 'evaluate' costs and benefits (CFTC standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: For agencies statutorily required to 'consider the costs and benefits' (e.g., CFTC under 7 U.S.C. § 19(a)(1)), the legal obligation is to evaluate costs and benefits; the judicially articulated standard can be relatively flexible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have observed that this statutory duty is 'not particularly demanding' — agencies need not always gather new market data or conduct empirical studies, but they must reasonably address uncertainty and not ignore pertinent cost/benefit considerations (e.g., extraterritorial impacts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage OIRA guidance/assistance where lawful (OIRA MOU practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent financial regulators can be informed by OIRA guidance and best practices and may enter MOUs to receive OIRA technical assistance during implementation and agency economic analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFTC–OIRA MOU described OIRA's role as providing 'technical assistance' informed by OIRA guidance and best practices, without establishing a supervisory OIRA review relationship; such collaboration can increase quantitative rigor but the scope was described in vague terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: FSOC coordination role to improve system-wide economic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A coordinating body (FSOC) should leverage cross-agency macroeconomic expertise to assess how individual rules affect the probability of serious negative economic consequences and to harmonize analytical approaches across financial regulators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FSOC is positioned to: identify systemic risks; facilitate information sharing and coordination among member agencies; identify regulatory gaps; recommend standards; establish subject-matter committees (e.g., Systemic Risk, Data) to promote shared responsibility and informal coordination. The article proposes FSOC as a model/hub for quantification and data to improve CBAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish formal coordination policies and adopt OMB analytical practices (GAO recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: FSOC and member agencies should adopt formal coordination policies and ensure specific practices from OMB regulatory analysis guidance are more fully incorporated into rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO has urged FSOC to strengthen accountability and collaboration (establish formal policies) and recommended that federal financial regulators better ensure OMB-style regulatory analysis practices are used; the FSOC broadly agreed with GAO’s conclusions.
